title: Best NVIDIA Graphics Card (2026): 7 RTX GPUs Ranked by Budget
description: The RTX 5070 is the best NVIDIA graphics card for most buyers: 12 GB, DLSS 4 and 250 W for $550–$650. 7 GeForce cards ranked, from the RTX 4060 to the 5090.
dek: Which GeForce card to buy in 2026, from the RTX 5060 to the RTX 5090, plus when an older RTX 40 card or a Radeon is the smarter buy.
about: NVIDIA was founded in 1993 by Jensen Huang, Chris Malachowsky and Curtis Priem, and it is headquartered in Santa Clara, California. Its GeForce 256, released in 1999, was marketed as the first GPU, and GeForce has been the best-selling line of PC graphics cards for most of the years since. NVIDIA designs the chips and sells Founders Edition cards, while partners such as ASUS, MSI, Gigabyte and Zotac build most GeForce cards on sale.

In 2018, the RTX 20 series added dedicated ray tracing and AI hardware, and with it DLSS, the upscaler that now shapes how many PC games are played. Data center chips for AI now bring in most of NVIDIA's revenue, but for gamers the current lineup is the RTX 50 series, built on the Blackwell architecture and launched in 2025.
intro: The GeForce RTX 5070 is the best NVIDIA graphics card for most people in 2026. At $550 to $650, it pairs 12 GB of GDDR7 with DLSS 4 and a 250 W rating, which makes it the most balanced RTX 50 card for high-refresh 1440p gaming.

This page ranks seven GeForce cards by what they deliver for the money, from the RTX 4060 for older budget builds to the RTX 5090. Each pick is matched to a resolution and budget, and the sections below cover RTX 40 cards, partner models, NVIDIA's weak spots and when AMD or Intel is the better buy.
quickAnswer: Buy the RTX 5070 ($550–$650) for 1440p. Step up to the RTX 5070 Ti ($750–$900) for 16 GB and 4K with DLSS. The RTX 5060 Ti 16GB ($430–$480) is the cheapest NVIDIA card with enough VRAM to age well. The RTX 5080 and 5090 suit 4K buyers with big budgets, and the RTX 5060 fits esports-only builds.

picks.label: Best NVIDIA Card Overall
picks.bestFor: 1440p gamers who want DLSS 4 and NVIDIA features at a mid-range price
picks.skipIf: you keep cards for many years and want 16 GB of VRAM
writeup: Within NVIDIA's lineup, the RTX 5070 is the card where price, speed and features line up best. Independent reviews put it roughly level with the RTX 4070 Super, so it runs most games at 1440p and high settings at high refresh rates, with DLSS 4 stretching that further. Its 250 W rating means a quality 650 W power supply is enough, and the two-slot Founders Edition fits compact cases.

The compromise is memory. Twelve gigabytes on a 192-bit bus covers 1440p today, but it is the smallest amount NVIDIA offers above the 60 class, and a few current games at maximum textures with ray tracing already push past it. If you keep a card for four or five years, that is the point to weigh. NVIDIA's own answer is the RTX 5070 Ti at about $200 more. AMD's is the 16 GB RX 9070 at a similar price, covered in our [RTX 5070 vs RX 9070](/compare/rtx-5070-vs-rx-9070/) comparison.

Ignore NVIDIA's launch claim of RTX 4090 performance, which leaned on Multi Frame Generation. Judge the 5070 as a fast 1440p card with the strongest feature set in its price range, and buy it close to $550.
pros: Runs on a 650 W power supply
cons: 12 GB is tight for maxed settings

picks.label: Best High-End NVIDIA
picks.bestFor: high-refresh 1440p and 4K gamers who want path tracing and 16 GB
picks.skipIf: you mostly play raster games and want the most frames per dollar
writeup: The RTX 5070 Ti is the NVIDIA card most high-end buyers should stop at. It uses a cut-down version of the RTX 5080's chip with the same 16 GB of GDDR7 on a 256-bit bus, and independent reviews place it close to the last-generation RTX 4080. That is enough for very high frame rates at 1440p and comfortable 4K play once DLSS is switched on.

Its value is clearest next to the card above it. The RTX 5080 is only about 15% faster in independent reviews but costs 30–45% more at street prices, which makes the 5070 Ti the better buy for nearly everyone shopping in this range. Our [RTX 5080 vs RTX 5070 Ti](/compare/rtx-5080-vs-rtx-5070-ti/) page breaks down the gap.

Where NVIDIA's premium pays off is heavy ray tracing and path tracing, plus CUDA support in Blender, video editors and local AI tools. For mostly raster gaming, AMD's RX 9070 XT trades blows with it for $100 to $150 less. Plan for a 750 W Gold power supply, and look for cards near the $749 launch price; above $900, the cheaper AMD card is hard to ignore.
cons: Costs more than the RX 9070 XT

picks.label: Best NVIDIA Under $500
picks.bestFor: 1080p and entry 1440p builds that need 16 GB and DLSS under $500
picks.skipIf: your board is PCIe 3.0 or you only care about raster frames per dollar
writeup: If your budget stops below $500, the RTX 5060 Ti 16GB is the GeForce card to buy. It is the cheapest current NVIDIA card with 16 GB of memory, which matters more than its modest speed gain over the RTX 4060 Ti. New games at high textures already overflow 8 GB at 1080p, and this card sidesteps that problem.

Its 4,608 CUDA cores and 448 GB/s of bandwidth make it a strong high-settings 1080p card and a workable 1440p card with DLSS. At 180 W, it suits small cases and 550 W power supplies, and most models use a single 8-pin plug.

Two cautions. First, make sure you get the 16 GB model; the 8 GB version shares the name and costs less but runs into memory limits. Second, the card uses an eight-lane PCIe 5.0 link, which is fine on PCIe 4.0 and 5.0 boards but loses a little on older PCIe 3.0 systems. AMD's RX 9060 XT 16GB offers similar raster speed for $50 to $80 less, so choose the NVIDIA card for DLSS coverage, ray tracing or CUDA apps.
pros: 180 W and a single 8-pin on most models
cons: Easy to confuse with the 8 GB model

picks.label: Best NVIDIA for 4K
picks.bestFor: 4K gamers who want more headroom than the 5070 Ti without RTX 5090 cost
picks.skipIf: you can find an RTX 5070 Ti near its launch price
writeup: The RTX 5080 is NVIDIA's second-fastest card and the most practical way into high-refresh 4K without paying RTX 5090 money. It has 10,752 CUDA cores and 16 GB of GDDR7 on a 256-bit bus, and independent reviews put it about 10–15% ahead of the RTX 4080 Super. With DLSS 4 and Multi Frame Generation, it handles 4K at high settings in most games.

The case against it is the 5070 Ti, which shares the same memory setup for roughly $250 to $400 less. Buy the 5080 only if you want the extra margin at 4K and accept weaker value per frame. It is rated at 360 W, and NVIDIA recommends an 850 W power supply.

If you are searching for the best RTX 5080 model, start with fit and price rather than factory overclocks. The Founders Edition is a compact two-slot design. Partner cards from ASUS, MSI, Gigabyte, Zotac and others differ mainly in cooler size, noise and extras such as a dual BIOS switch on some models, while factory overclocks usually add only a few percent. The cheapest model with a cooler your case can hold is usually the right buy.
pros: 16 GB of GDDR7 on a 256-bit bus
cons: Only about 15% faster than the 5070 Ti

picks.label: Fastest NVIDIA GPU
picks.bestFor: 4K high-refresh gaming with every setting on, and local AI work
picks.skipIf: you play at 1440p or need to keep total build cost reasonable
writeup: The RTX 5090 is the fastest graphics card you can buy, and nothing from AMD or Intel competes with it. It carries 21,760 CUDA cores and 32 GB of GDDR7 on a 512-bit bus, and independent reviews put it roughly 25–35% ahead of the RTX 4090 at 4K, with the most benefit in path-traced games and large local AI models.

Everything about owning one is expensive. Street prices run $2,000 to $2,700, about twice an RTX 5080, for a gap that is large at 4K but nowhere near double. NVIDIA rates the card at 575 W and recommends a 1,000 W power supply. Owners have reported melted 16-pin connectors, so use a fully seated native 12V-2x6 cable from an ATX 3.1 unit and avoid sharp bends near the plug.

Buy the 5090 for 4K at 144 Hz or higher with every setting on, or for AI and rendering work that needs 32 GB. At 1440p, much of what you pay for goes unused. For gaming alone, the 5080 or 5070 Ti covers almost every real need for far less, as our [RTX 5090 vs RTX 5080](/compare/rtx-5090-vs-rtx-5080/) page shows.
pros: No rival from AMD or Intel

picks.label: Best for Esports Builds
picks.bestFor: competitive shooters and older games at 1080p on a tight budget
picks.skipIf: you play new single-player games at high textures
writeup: The RTX 5060 is the realistic entry point to NVIDIA's current lineup. Independent reviews put it around 20% ahead of the RTX 4060, and with 3,840 CUDA cores, GDDR7 memory and DLSS 4, it runs esports games at very high frame rates and most new releases at 1080p with medium to high settings.

The problem is its 8 GB of VRAM. A growing list of new games exceed 8 GB at high textures even at 1080p, and frame generation adds to the load. When the card runs out, stutter follows, and the eight-lane PCIe link makes that worse on PCIe 3.0 boards. Lower textures fix it, at a cost you accept on day one.

That makes it a narrow pick. It suits competitive shooters, MOBAs and older games, and its 145 W draw is easy on small power supplies and compact cases. For anyone who plays new single-player releases, the RTX 5060 Ti 16GB is worth the extra $100 to $150, and our [RTX 5060 vs RX 9060 XT 16GB](/compare/rtx-5060-vs-rx-9060-xt-16gb/) comparison covers the Radeon alternative.

picks.label: Best Older Budget Pick
picks.bestFor: low-power 1080p builds when the price sits clearly below the RTX 5060
picks.skipIf: the RTX 5060 costs about the same
writeup: The RTX 4060 is the one RTX 40 card that still makes sense for a budget build, and only at the right price. It has 8 GB of GDDR6, 3,072 CUDA cores and a 115 W rating, which makes it one of NVIDIA's most power-efficient budget cards, and compact single-fan versions fit small-form-factor cases.

It also keeps most of NVIDIA's software. RTX 40 cards support DLSS 4 upscaling with the newer transformer model and single Frame Generation; what they lack is Multi Frame Generation, which is exclusive to the RTX 50 series. For a 1080p esports or older-games machine, that hardly matters.

The catch is that the RTX 5060 is about 20% faster for similar money and has the same 8 GB limit. Buy the 4060 only when it sells clearly below the 5060, when you find a used one from a trusted seller, or when its lower power draw matters in a small build. Like the 5060, it uses an eight-lane PCIe link, so it loses a little in older PCIe 3.0 boards.

ranking.intro: These rankings draw on NVIDIA's published specifications, independent reviews from established hardware outlets and owner reports on drivers, noise and connectors. None of these cards were bench-tested by us. We ranked each on how well it serves its target resolution and budget, with extra weight on VRAM because it decides how long a card stays useful.
criteria: Relative results in independent reviews at the resolution each card is sold for, not NVIDIA's frame generation claims.
Whether the memory covers new games at high textures today and for several years, which is why 8 GB cards rank lower.
Current price bands against the next NVIDIA card up and down, and against AMD and Intel rivals.
Board power, recommended PSU, connector type and card size.
DLSS 4, Multi Frame Generation, ray tracing strength, NVENC and CUDA support.
ranking.why: The RTX 5070 won because it delivers the most NVIDIA speed and features per dollar at 1440p, the resolution most buyers now play at.

mentions.text: The RTX 4070 has 12 GB of GDDR6X and a 200 W rating, and it is still a capable 1440p card. It trails the RTX 5070 and lacks Multi Frame Generation, so it makes sense only used, at a price well below a new 5070 and from a seller with a clear history.

mentions.name: NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5050
mentions.text: The RTX 5050 is the cheapest RTX 50 card, with 8 GB of GDDR6 and a 130 W rating. It brings DLSS 4 and Multi Frame Generation to a lower price, but it is clearly slower than the RTX 5060 while sharing the same 8 GB limit, so the small saving rarely pays off.

mentions.name: NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5060 Ti 8GB
mentions.text: The 8 GB RTX 5060 Ti uses the same chip as the 16 GB model for less money, but it hits the same memory wall as the RTX 5060 in new games. Because the 16 GB card costs only modestly more, we would skip the 8 GB version, especially for 1440p or an older PCIe 3.0 system.

sections.h: Which RTX 50 Card Is Right for Your Resolution?
body: Match the card to your monitor first. Resolution and refresh rate decide how much GPU you need far more than game genre does.

For 1080p, the RTX 5060 Ti 16GB is the safe choice; the RTX 5060 is fine only if you stick to esports titles. For 1440p, the RTX 5070 covers high refresh rates in most games, and the 5070 Ti adds margin for maxed settings and ray tracing. For 4K, start at the 5070 Ti with DLSS, move to the 5080 for high refresh rates, and save the 5090 for path tracing or AI work. Use our [PSU calculator](/tools/psu-calculator/) once you have picked a card.

sections.h: What Is the Best-Selling RTX 50 Series GPU?
body: NVIDIA does not publish sales by model, so there is no official answer. The best public signal is the monthly Steam Hardware Survey, and as with every recent GeForce generation, 60-class and 70-class cards account for most RTX 50 owners there, while the RTX 5080 and 5090 make up a small share. Retailer best-seller lists point the same way.

Popular is not the same as best. The RTX 5060 sells largely on price and through prebuilt PCs, but its 8 GB of VRAM makes it a weaker long-term buy than the 5060 Ti 16GB or the 5070. If you want the RTX 50 card that most buyers should end up with, it is the 5070 at 1440p and the 5060 Ti 16GB below $500.

sections.h: Is the RTX 40 Series Still Worth Buying?
body: Mostly no, if you are buying new. NVIDIA has wound down RTX 40 production, and remaining new stock tends to sit near the price of the faster RTX 50 card that replaced it. The RTX 4060 is the exception worth watching, but only when it sells clearly below the RTX 5060.

Used cards are a different story. RTX 40 cards support DLSS 4 upscaling and single Frame Generation, so they keep most of NVIDIA's software. A used RTX 4070 Super or RTX 4080 can be good value if it undercuts a new 5070 or 5070 Ti by a clear margin. Ask for the receipt, check whether the warranty transfers, and inspect the 16-pin connector on high-end cards for discoloration.

NVIDIA's biggest advantage is software. DLSS is supported in far more games than AMD's FSR 4 or Intel's XeSS, and NVIDIA's override settings in the NVIDIA App can apply the newer DLSS model to many older DLSS titles. Ray tracing and especially path tracing still run better on GeForce cards at every price point.

Outside gaming, CUDA remains the default for many creative and AI tools, and the NVENC encoder is widely used for streaming. That makes a GeForce card the low-risk choice if your PC does more than play games, and the RTX 5090 gives NVIDIA the only answer at the very top.

Memory is the most common complaint. NVIDIA still sells 8 GB cards in 2026 and puts 12 GB on the RTX 5070, while AMD offers 16 GB on similarly priced cards. Street prices have also sat above launch prices for much of the RTX 50 generation, especially for the 5090.

The launch year had rough spots. In early 2025, owners reported black screens and crashes with early RTX 50 drivers, which later releases addressed. NVIDIA confirmed that a small share of early RTX 5090, 5080 and 5070 Ti cards shipped with fewer ROPs than specified and offered replacements. The RTX 50 series also dropped support for 32-bit PhysX, which affects some older games that used it.
Finally, high-end cards rely on the 16-pin 12V-2x6 connector, and melted-connector reports on the RTX 4090 and RTX 5090 mean cable care matters more than it did with 8-pin plugs.

NVIDIA wins on features and the high end; AMD wins on VRAM and raster performance per dollar; Intel competes only in the budget class. AMD's RX 9070 XT trades blows with the RTX 5070 Ti in raster games for $100 to $150 less, and the RX 9060 XT 16GB undercuts the RTX 5060 Ti 16GB. Intel's Arc B580 offers 12 GB for less than an RTX 5060 but loses speed on older CPUs because of driver overhead.

If you play path-traced games, use CUDA software or want the widest DLSS support, pay the NVIDIA premium. If you mostly play raster games, compare the Radeon card at the same price first; our [best AMD graphics card](/best-amd-graphics-card/) guide covers that lineup.

body: Skip NVIDIA if your budget is fixed and you play mostly raster games: the RX 9070 XT, RX 9070 and RX 9060 XT 16GB give you more VRAM and similar frame rates for less. Skip it too if you want 16 GB for around $550 to $650, since NVIDIA's card at that price has 12 GB.

Linux and SteamOS gamers often find AMD's open-source drivers simpler to live with, though NVIDIA's Linux support has improved. For a very cheap new PC around a recent CPU, Intel's Arc B580 is worth a look below $300.

mistakes: Buying an 8 GB card for new games

The RTX 5060, RTX 5050 and 8 GB RTX 5060 Ti all run short of memory in some new games at high textures, even at 1080p. If you play recent single-player releases, the RTX 5060 Ti 16GB costs more but avoids stutter and texture compromises.
Judging cards by frame generation charts

NVIDIA's marketing often compares cards with Multi Frame Generation on, which multiplies displayed frames but adds latency and does not reflect native speed. Compare cards on independent reviews of native and upscaled performance, and treat frame generation as a bonus for high-refresh monitors.
Paying RTX 5080 money for a small gain

The RTX 5080 is only about 15% faster than the RTX 5070 Ti in independent reviews but costs 30–45% more. Unless you need every bit of 4K headroom or the 5070 Ti is out of stock, the cheaper card is the smarter buy.
Reusing a worn or bent 16-pin cable

High-end RTX 50 cards draw a lot of current through one 12V-2x6 plug. Use a native cable from an ATX 3.1 power supply, push it in until it is fully seated, avoid sharp bends near the card, and retire old adapters that have been plugged in many times.

Premium partner models often cost $100 or more over base models for factory overclocks worth a few percent. Pay extra only for things you will notice, such as a quieter cooler, a size that fits your case or a longer warranty.
bottomLine: The RTX 5070 is the best NVIDIA graphics card for most buyers at $550 to $650, with DLSS 4 and the speed for high-refresh 1440p. Step up to the RTX 5070 Ti for 16 GB and 4K, choose the RTX 5060 Ti 16GB below $500, and buy the 5080 or 5090 only for demanding 4K or AI work. Avoid 8 GB cards for new games.

faqs.q: What is the best NVIDIA graphics card right now?
faqs.a: The RTX 5070 is the best NVIDIA graphics card for most people in 2026. It costs $550 to $650 and offers roughly RTX 4070 Super speed, 12 GB of GDDR7 and DLSS 4. The RTX 5090 is faster, but at $2,000 or more it suits only 4K with every setting on or AI work.

faqs.q: Which RTX 50 series card is the best value?
faqs.a: The RTX 5070 and the RTX 5060 Ti 16GB are the best-value RTX 50 cards. The 5070 gives the most performance per dollar for 1440p, while the 5060 Ti 16GB is the cheapest card with 16 GB for 1080p and entry 1440p. The RTX 5080 is the weakest value because it costs far more than the 5070 Ti for a small gain.

faqs.q: Is the RTX 5080 worth it over the RTX 5070 Ti?
faqs.a: For most buyers, no. Independent reviews put the RTX 5080 about 15% ahead of the RTX 5070 Ti, while it costs 30–45% more at street prices. Both have 16 GB of GDDR7 on a 256-bit bus. The 5080 makes sense if you want maximum 4K headroom or the 5070 Ti is unavailable near its launch price.

faqs.q: What is the best RTX 5080 graphics card model?
faqs.a: The best RTX 5080 model is usually the cheapest one with a cooler that fits your case. Factory overclocks on premium partner cards add only a few percent. The Founders Edition is a compact two-slot design, while larger partner coolers from ASUS, MSI, Gigabyte and others tend to run quieter. Check card length and slot width before buying.

faqs.q: Is NVIDIA better than AMD for gaming?
faqs.a: NVIDIA is better for ray tracing, DLSS game support and the high end, while AMD is better for VRAM and raster performance per dollar. Radeon cards like the RX 9070 XT match NVIDIA in raster games for less. If you play path-traced games or use CUDA apps, NVIDIA is worth the premium.

faqs.q: Should I buy an RTX 4060 or an RTX 5060?
faqs.a: Buy the RTX 5060 if the two cost about the same. Independent reviews put it around 20% ahead of the RTX 4060, and it adds Multi Frame Generation. Both have 8 GB of VRAM and an eight-lane PCIe link. The RTX 4060 makes sense only when it is clearly cheaper or you need its lower 115 W power draw.

Yes, partly. RTX 40 cards support DLSS 4 upscaling with the newer transformer model and single Frame Generation. Multi Frame Generation, which inserts up to three generated frames per rendered frame, is exclusive to the RTX 50 series. RTX 20 and 30 cards also get the improved upscaling, but no frame generation.
